implementation_notes: kotlinx.coroutines supplies the machinery: suspend is language syntax, but the API surface lives in the library - async {} starts the work and returns a Deferred that 'represents an eventual result', await() suspends the caller until it is ready, and invokeOnCompletion registers a completion handler that also receives the failure cause, which is the event callback in coroutine form. Structured concurrency keeps the operation inside the caller's scope, so joining, failure propagation and cancellation come for free; hand-rolled event classes are unnecessary, and blocking calls belong on Dispatchers.IO.
pitfalls: An async{} failure is delivered only to an await(), a parent scope or an invokeOnCompletion handler; an unobserved failure is lost and an un-awaited Deferred dies with its scope.
GlobalScope (or a scope that outlives the caller) breaks structured concurrency: the completion can arrive after the consumer is gone and cancellation no longer propagates.
Blocking calls inside a coroutine clog the dispatcher thread - use withContext(Dispatchers.IO) for blocking work.

variants.name: suspendCancellableCoroutine / callbackFlow bridging a callback API
variants.implementation_notes: When the completion arrives from a foreign callback API, the bridge is explicit: suspendCancellableCoroutine stores the continuation and the API's completion callback resumes it exactly once with a value or an exception ('resume coroutine with a value provided by the callback'), while cancellation is wired to the API's own cancel. For many events - progress plus completion - callbackFlow wraps the subscription and awaitClose releases the listener when the consumer stops. This is the direct analogue of the classic event object, kept inside suspend-land so callers never see the callback.
variants.code_sketch:
suspend fun fetchReport(): Report = suspendCancellableCoroutine { cont ->
    val sub = api.startReport(
        onDone  = { r -> cont.resume(r) },              // exactly once
        onError = { e -> cont.resumeWithException(e) })
    cont.invokeOnCancellation { sub.cancel() }           // cooperative stop
}
pitfalls: Resuming the continuation twice - or never - is a bug the library only sometimes catches: the callback contract must guarantee exactly one terminal call.
Callback invocations arrive on the API's own thread: resuming from there is allowed, but touching coroutine-confined state requires withContext or a channel.
awaitClose must release the underlying listener/registration, otherwise callbackFlow leaks the subscription after the collector leaves.
